title: Where black bands ate and slept in the segregated era
summary: Hinton and Wilson recall the black restaurants and rooming houses every band knew, such as Mom Sutton's and Mother's Lunch, and the Negro districts of Detroit and Indianapolis.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Sure. And you know, one thing that most people don't really know, if it's possible for you to talk about, Teddy -- is being in black bands in that era before 1954, with the segregation thing. How we survived without animosity and without anger in the places where we had to stay and the places we had to eat.
Now all over America, every black musician knew where to go to eat--- in every band would have to eat in places like Uncle Henry's in Cincinnati, do you remember Mom Sutton's in Atlanta, Georgia?
Mother Hadlows's in Philadelphia -- you remember these places?
Of course in the cities, though, you'd have a whole Negro community, like in Detroit, all up and down Hastings or St. Antoine Street or on the west side around Milford

and Westwood. That area was loaded with little Negro restaurants, where we would risk getting refused in white restaurants in those days -- hotels and restaurants when we traveled, so the best bet was just to go to the ghetto district where we knew the hotel situation, or rooming house or restaurant to eat or sleep.
Yeah. The Palm Leaf Hotel in Birmingham.
Well, there were so many. It was a special life for us, and yet we survived it. We had to get rooms --
Like in Indianapolis, in the Negro ghetto district, the rooming facilities and food --
And so we knew that in each town so we could take care of ourselves.
